types.standards_anchor: ASME BPVC Section VIII marking where the vessel is code-stamped, plus hydronic air-control conventions: the record needs the separation method (centrifugal/tangential, coalescing-medium, or in-line), the design flow and connection size, the working pressure and temperature, the vent/air-elimination arrangement, the blowdown or strainer provision, and whether a dirt separator function is combined. NOTE: this anchor is WEAKER than the NETA and NFPA ones - manufacturer convention governs much of it. Flag any field that is firm convention rather than standard.
types.note: Kept to 10 — an air separator is a vessel with a few connections and an air-elimination fitting, not a machine with performance curves. The anchor is manufacturer/hydronic convention more than a hard standard, so most fields here (separation method, blowdown provision, combined dirt-separator function, insulation) are firm/industry convention rather than code-driven; only Vessel Design Pressure ties directly to an ASME code stamp where one applies. Left out things like tank volume or shell diameter — they exist on the shop drawing but nobody references them again once the unit is accepted.

fields.reasoning: centrifugal/tangential, coalescing-medium, or in-line — the basic design choice the schedule specifies and the shop drawing confirms
inlet/outlet pipe size; NPS is written the same both systems per convention
the duty flow the separator is sized against; flow rate genuinely swaps unit systems
system operating pressure the vessel must hold; recorded against the nameplate/ASME rating at install
hydronic system operating temperature the separator is rated for
automatic float-type air vent vs. manual vent valve, and its location — a physically checkable arrangement
whether a blowdown valve or strainer basket is provided for debris removal, per the hydronic air-control convention
many air separators are sold as combination air/dirt units; whether this one is affects TAB and maintenance expectations
the ASME-stamped or manufacturer-rated pressure of the vessel itself, distinct from system working pressure
whether the vessel is field- or factory-insulated; a visual check at the unit

types.standards_anchor: ASME A17.1 / CSA B44, Safety Code for Elevators and Escalators - the harmonized North American code, adopted in Ontario by the TSSA (B44:19 or :22). The commissioning record needs the machine arrangement (traction/MRL/hydraulic), rated capacity, rated speed, travel/rise, number of stops and openings, controller and door-operator type, and - the part that matters to an integrated test - FIREFIGHTERS EMERGENCY OPERATION: Phase I recall (designated and alternate landing, initiating device) and Phase II in-car operation, plus emergency/standby power operation and the fire-alarm interface. Phase I/II TEST RESULTS are test-record data, not nameplate fields.
types.note: Kept to configuration facts a technician can read off the car, controller nameplate, or shop drawing — Phase I/II fields record the arrangement, not the test result, which belongs to FPT and the Issues Log, not the nameplate. No field here duplicates the ASME/CSA plate data already carried by __base.

fields.reasoning: traction / MRL / hydraulic — the basic classification the code and every later check hangs off
A17.1/B44 nameplate requirement; capacity is written in kg on Canadian equipment plates and lb on US-manufactured ones
governs the code-required speed test; genuinely swaps units between m/s and fpm depending on manufacturer origin
total rise; fixes hoistway length and confirms against the architectural section
a plain count, needed to cross-check landing and opening records
distinct from stops where front/rear openings exist; both counts matter to the door-operation test plan
microprocessor/relay-logic and manufacturer platform; what the FPT script is written against
governs the door reversal and dwell-time checks the code requires
A17.1 firefighters' recall — the primary recall floor, fixed by the fire-alarm interface design
the backup recall floor used when the designated landing itself is in alarm
which detector/signal triggers recall — the fact the integrated fire-alarm test is run against
in-car firefighters' operation switch, a physical installed fact rather than a spec value
automatic transfer, single-car sequential, or none — determines the standby-power integrated test
hardwired vs. monitoring-module connection to the FACP, the point the ILS coordination test verifies

types.standards_anchor: AMCA 500-L (laboratory methods of testing louvers) with AMCA 511 certified ratings, and AMCA 550 for wind-driven rain where it applies: a louver is rated on FREE AREA, on the beginning point of water penetration at a stated free-area velocity, and on pressure drop at a stated velocity. The record also needs the nominal size, blade/frame type and material, finish, screen arrangement, and - where the louver serves a smoke or fire application - its ULC listing and damper interface.
types.note: Left out a separate 'actual free area' area figure (sq ft/m2) alongside the % rating - one free-area field is what a CxA reads off the schedule, and a second number invites confusion about which is being recorded. Also left out AMCA 550 wind-driven-rain class as a routine field: it only applies where the project specifies it, and a convention-not-standard field for an occasional case is better added on the project than carried on every louver.

fields.reasoning: the width x height a louver is scheduled and ordered by; a length dimension, so it takes the imperial counterpart
the core AMCA 500-L rating a louver is selected against
the stated velocity at which the pressure-drop and water-penetration ratings apply - a velocity genuinely swaps units
the AMCA 500-L resistance figure tied to the rated velocity above
the AMCA 500-L wind-driven water rating - the velocity at which penetration begins
drainable, storm-resistant, fixed or adjustable - fixes what was actually ordered vs installed
mill, anodized, painted - visually confirmable on site
bird screen, insect screen or none - a distinct field from the blade itself
whether the louver is paired with a control or fire/smoke damper behind it
only meaningful where the louver serves a fire or smoke application, but the anchor calls it out explicitly and it is verifiable from the nameplate/label
